artworks.title: Pelops and Hippodamia
artworks.description: Kaselowsky's mural for Berlin's Neues Museum stages the chariot race that made Hippodamia a bride and a queen: she rides with Pelops while her father Oenomaus pursues — the contest whose prize was her hand and whose aftermath named the Peloponnese. Nineteenth-century historicism freezes her at the hinge of Olympia's foundation myth, the princess whose marriage founded a cursed dynasty.

artworks.title: Terracotta plaque with Pelops and Hippodamia
artworks.description: This Augustan or Julio-Claudian Campana plaque in the Metropolitan Museum of Art shows Hippodamia beside Pelops in the chariot — the couple whose race against Oenomaus became Olympia's founding legend. About 38 cm high, the Roman domestic relief carries Pisa's bridal prize into villa decoration, Hippodamia as the living stake of the contest.

artworks.title: Sarcophagus of Pelops and Hippodamia
artworks.description: This Roman sarcophagus in the Tipaza Archaeological Museum retells the chariot race for Hippodamia in continuous relief — horses, drivers, and the bridal prize carved for a North African tomb. Imperial workshops favoured the story as victorious love and dynastic founding; the Tipaza chest shows how far Oenomaus' daughter travelled as an emblem of the won bride.

popCulture.title: Temple of Zeus, Olympia
popCulture.description: The east pediment of Zeus's temple staged the oath before Pelops' race for Hippodamia — Pausanias places her among the figures whose wedding founded the Olympic contest.

popCulture.title: Peloponnese
popCulture.description: The peninsula took Pelops' name after he won Hippodamia — her bridal race is the myth that still labels the southern Greek landmass.
